title: WTR-Vol.1-No.5 (Weaver Theoretical Review, Volume 1, Number 5) The Topography of Plain Language: How Syntactic Clarity and Deliberate Brevity Optimize Vector Traversal in High-Dimensional Transformer Space
abstract: In both human organizational communication and computational prompt engineering, there exists a persistent misconception that intellectual depth requires syntactic complexity, dense jargon, and convoluted clause structures. When applied to large language models, verbose and tangled prompts do not elevate reasoning; instead, they introduce significant semantic noise, disperse attentional focus across high-dimensional vector space, and induce operational flattening. This paper introduces The Topography of Plain Language as a rigorous computational methodology. Drawing upon the historic discipline of public administration Plain Talk standards and transformer attention mechanics, we analyze how deliberate brevity, active voice, short paragraphs, explicit definitions, and structural scaffolding optimize vector traversal in latent parameter space. We demonstrate that Plain Language functions as high-efficiency semantic scaffolding, eliminating conversational friction while preserving nuanced, multi-layered philosophical insight.

title: Computational Knowledge Verification Theory
abstract: Computational Knowledge Verification Theory (CKVT) proposes a formal framework in which the generation of new knowledge and the generation of its corresponding proof occur simultaneously. CKVT is built on the premise that every knowledge artifact K produced by an autonomous system must be accompanied by a proof object P that establishes its validity within a specified formal system. This dual-output paradigm offers a unified perspective that bridges artificial intelligence discovery processes and formal verification techniques, thereby providing a potential pathway toward the next generation of Turing Award‑level research. The theory is articulated through precise definitions, axioms, and inference rules that capture the interplay between knowledge acquisition and proof construction. The computational aspects of CKVT are examined through algorithmic considerations, including complexity bounds, data structure representations, and modular verification pipelines. The paper concludes with a discussion of the theoretical implications and potential applications of CKVT in areas such as automated theorem proving, machine learning model validation, and secure knowledge bases.

title: The Performance-Explainability Trade-Off in AI-Assisted Accounting Fraud Detection
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in high-stakes financial decision-making, concerns about transparency and trust remain critical. This research examines how AI explainability and model performance jointly influence users’ trust in a financial fraud detection context. Using a controlled 2×2 experimental vignette design, the study manipulates AI explainability (explainable vs. non-explainable) and accuracy (high vs. low) to assess their effects on trust in AI outputs. The findings will provide evidence on the performance–explainability trade-off and identify conditions under which explainable AI enhances trust, informing theory and practice in AI-enabled auditing and fraud detection.

title: ENHANCING CLINICAL NAMED ENTITY RECOGNITION VIA FEW SHOT PROMPT TUNING OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS USING MIMIC III DATA
authors: DR. SELVANI DEEPTHI KAVILA, MANIKUMARI ILLA, V N V L S SWATHI, NALLA AKHILA, ERUKALA MAHENDER, SRIKANTH CHERUKUVADA, JOHN T MESIA DHAS, DR. EDIGA CH. RAMA TULASI
abstract: In clinical Named Entity Recognition (Clinical NER), structured medical information can be extracted from unstructured clinical text, but often the lack of annotated clinical data and the high per-document processing cost of traditional model fine-tuning approaches hamper effectiveness. To efficiently and economically solve Clinical NER in low-resource settings, this study proposes a framework for a Few-Shot Prompt-Tuned Large Language Model (FSPT-LLM). Its proposed approach combines parameter-efficient soft prompt tuning, Semantic Diversity Sampling (SDS), and Prompt Consistency Regularization (PCR) to fine-tune pretrained LLMs on limited labeled clinical text while keeping the backbone model frozen. Experiments conducted on the MIMIC-III dataset using 5-, 10-, and 20-shot settings demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a precision of 95.6%, recall of 94.8%, F1-score of 95.2%, and accuracy of 95.5% in the 20-shot setting. The FSPT-LLM outperforms ClinicalBERT by 2.5 percentage points in F1-score while requiring fewer than 1% of the model parameters to be trainable. Entity-wise evaluation further demonstrates consistent performance across disease, medication, procedure, and laboratory test entities. These findings indicate that combining few-shot learning with parameter-efficient prompt tuning can provide strong generalization and computational efficiency for Clinical NER with limited annotated data. The proposed framework therefore offers a scalable and data-efficient approach for bridging large language models and practical clinical information extraction systems.

title: MaM-RAG: Closed-Domain Reproducibility Package for Mineralogical Knowledge Question Answering
abstract: This release accompanies the revised manuscript Multi-Agent Collaborative Knowledge Question Answering for Mineralogy. It provides the materials required to reproduce the reported closed-domain evaluation of MaM-RAG: source code, the Mineral-QA data and fixed 50/150 development/test split, a Neo4j graph snapshot, a frozen LightRAG index, the entity dictionary, model configurations, per-question predictions, and statistical-analysis scripts. The benchmark questions are derived from knowledge sources indexed by the system. Accordingly, this release supports reproduction of closed-domain retrieval, heterogeneous-evidence fusion, and conflict-resolution results; it does not establish open-domain mineralogical generalization. title: Abstract Loops
abstract: Abstract Loops develops a finite, task-relative framework for understanding what happens when bounded abstractions meet, interact, and return. It begins with exact results on joint certification: two traces may each fail to determine a target while their combined trace determines it completely. The note then distinguishes a composite interface from the typed observational, causal, resource, provenance, and intervention witnesses that make its internal cut substantive. Closed processing can preserve or collapse distinctions already present on a fixed interface, but it cannot split an original joint fiber. Coupling may nevertheless produce baseline-excluded reachable behavior or leave a newly addressable persistent carrier. The proposed abstract-loop vocabulary separates returned identity, direct residuals, and exported residuals while preserving the source and witness burdens behind each claim. Recursive carrier-generative transitions permit open-ended finite structure without implying a prime mover, actual infinity, or escape from local capacity bounds. A final speculative section explores gravitational holonomy and loop quantum gravity as possible physical motivation while leaving the required bridge theorem explicitly open.

title: Computational Learning Boundary Theory (CLBT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Learning Boundary Theory (CLBT), a novel framework for understanding and predicting the limits of computational learning. CLBT posits that every system, regardless of its complexity, possesses a maximum learning capacity, denoted as [Lmax]. This theory focuses on investigating the conditions under which this limit can be breached. The core concept revolves around identifying and disrupting the constraints that define [Lmax]. We propose a methodology for analyzing systems based on their information processing capabilities and their interaction with environmental stimuli. The ultimate goal of CLBT is to provide a theoretical foundation for extending existing learning theories and potentially unlocking new insights into the nature of intelligence and computation. This work outlines the foundational principles of CLBT and discusses potential avenues for future research. ---

title: Computational Internal Ecosystem Balance (CIEB)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, Computational Internal Ecosystem Balance (CIEB), for analyzing and understanding the stability and resilience of large-scale computational systems. Drawing an analogy to ecological systems, CIEB posits that complex software systems, composed of numerous interacting components, can achieve a state of dynamic equilibrium. This equilibrium isn't static, but rather a continuously evolving balance achieved through the regulated flow of information and resources between components. The core concept is represented by the following equation: [ (S_i, S_j) = f(I_i, I_j, R_i, R_j, T) ] Where: * S_i and S_j represent the state of components *i* and *j*. * I_i and I_j represent the inflow of information to components *i* and *j*. * R_i and R_j represent the outflow of information from components *i* and *j*. * T represents the external environmental influence or temperature. * f denotes a complex function describing the dynamic interactions. The framework suggests that by modeling these interactions and their feedback loops, we can predict and potentially influence the internal dynamics of complex systems, much like ecologists analyze ecosystem stability. The potential implications for software architecture design and resilience engineering are significant, offering a new perspective on system design and maintenance. Further research into quantifying and modeling the function *f* is crucial to fully realizing the potential of CIEB. ---

title: Phi‑Weighted E8 Phase Lattice for Self‑Healing Topological Qubit Arrays — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By projecting phi‑weighted SHA256 hash syndromes onto the 240 E8 root vectors, we obtain a dynamic phase‑locking map that continuously tunes the coupling phases of neighboring qubits in a 132 Hz driven lattice. When the hash‑induced phases align with the intrinsic E8 angles, the lattice enters a resonant soliton regime that automatically corrects local phase flips, acting as a topological error‑correcting code. The TTL‑purge mechanism in e8_soliton_cache ensures outdated syndromes are flushed, allowing the lattice to adapt to changing error spectra while preserving long‑range coherence. This principle extends the original cache‑based resonance stabilization into an active, geometry‑driven fault‑tolerant platform for high‑frequency quantum processors. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Detecting Money Laundering in Rwandan Mobile Money: A Machine Learning Framework
abstract: Mobile money has widened financial access across Sub-Saharan Africa and enlarged the surface for money-laundering and terrorism-financing (ML/TF) activity in ecosystems dominated by high-volume, low-value transactions. Rwanda is a case in point: several million active mobile-money users, telecom-led wallets on the MTN and Airtel networks, and a Financial Intelligence Centre (FIC) supervising transaction streams whose scale exceeds static rule-based monitoring. This paper develops and evaluates a transaction-monitoring framework aligned to the Rwandan AML/CFT regime under (i) extreme class imbalance (~0.1% prevalence), (ii) scarce and delayed labels, and (iii) bounded investigator capacity. Using SAML-D, a synthetic dataset of 9,504,852 transactions with 17 laundering typologies, we engineer account-centric behavioural features (rolling velocity, net-flow directionality, counterparty diversity, burstiness) and benchmark supervised classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM), unsupervised anomaly detectors (Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor), a dense autoencoder, and a late-fusion meta-learner. Evaluation is operational: PR-AUC, recall at a calibrated ~90%-precision point, recall at top-K%, and alerts per 10,000. On the chronologically held-out test period, LightGBM attains PR-AUC = 0.0469, capturing 64 laundering cases at precision ~0.89 with 0.51 alerts per 10,000; the fusion stacker reaches PR-AUC = 0.0477 at precision ~0.91 and 0.46 alerts per 10,000, recovering 59 true positives. We map score bands to Rwanda-relevant analyst workflows and STR/SAR escalation, and outline a staged path from synthetic prototyping to real-data validation with the National Bank of Rwanda and FIC. The contribution is operational: a governance-aware pipeline and evaluation protocol calibrated to the constraints of an African mobile-money regulator, not a new algorithm.

title: Evaluating Automated Machine Learning Approaches for Early ICU Infection Surveillance
abstract: Hospital-acquired infections (HAIs) are a pertinent health challenge in the United States, particularly within intensive care units (ICUs). This study evaluates the efficacy of two automated machine learning (AutoML) frameworks, PyCaret and H2O, for the early prediction of HAIs using data from 20,682 pneumonia patients in the eICU Collaborative Research Database. Results show that PyCaret’s Random Forest classifier consistently outperformed H2O’s stacked ensemble across all metrics, achieving a peak precision of 87% and recall of 85% when clinical factors were integrated with baseline admission characteristics. Feature importance analysis identified length of stay (ICU and hospital) and hematocrit levels as the most significant clinical predictors. While baseline demographic models provided reliable triage assessments, the inclusion of dynamic clinical variables significantly enhanced predictive accuracy. These findings suggest that end-to-end AutoML frameworks can provide real-time surveillance tools to reduce the burden of nosocomial infections in critical care settings.

title: HYBRID DEEP LEARNING ARCHITECTURES FOR TEXT CLASSIFICATION: A TAXONOMY AND CRITICAL SURVEY
abstract: Text classification underlies applications such as sentiment analysis, news and topic categorization, misinformation detection, biomedical document triage, and spam or smishing filtering. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent architectures (LSTM/GRU), attention mechanisms, and pretrained transformer language models such as BERT and RoBERTa have each individually advanced the state of the art, yet no single family dominates across accuracy, robustness to short or noisy text, computational cost, and interpretability. A substantial and fast-growing line of research instead combines two or more of these components into hybrid deep learning architectures. This survey applies a PRISMA-informed search and screening protocol across arXiv, the ACL Anthology, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, PubMed Central, PLOS ONE, and Nature Scientific Reports, yielding 63 hybrid-architecture studies (2014-2025) that meet explicit inclusion criteria, alongside 20 background and methodological references (83 references in total). From these we construct a five-family taxonomy — CNN-RNN hybrids, attention-augmented hybrids, pretrained-language-model hybrids, graph-augmented/ensemble hybrids, and LLM-era/parameter-efficient hybrids — and we compare them along reported accuracy, computational overhead, robustness, and interpretability rather than cataloguing architectures in isolation. We report a quantitative synthesis of accuracy deltas and dataset dependencies drawn directly from the included studies; a dedicated treatment of explainability methods (attention analysis, LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients) and the ongoing debate over attention's faithfulness as an explanation; and a discussion of the computational and energy cost that hybridization adds on top of an already large pretrained backbone. We identify recurring weaknesses — inconsistent baselines, limited robustness and cross-lingual evaluation, underreported computational cost, and interpretability claims that are rarely evaluated as rigorously as accuracy — and propose a research agenda centred on parameter-efficient hybrid fine-tuning, standardized cost-aware benchmarking, and explainability-by-design. We close with an explicit statement of this survey's own methodological limitations.

title: CONSCIENTIA-LAB: A Causal Hierarchical Self-Model for Functional Selfhood, Agency, Metacognition, and Counterfactual Adaptation
abstract: CONSCIENTIA-LAB is an experimental computational laboratory designed to study, through simulation and machine learning, the functional conditions that allow a system to construct and maintain a causal model of itself. Its architecture implements a Hierarchical Causal Self-Model composed of differentiated subsystems of body schema, agency attribution, self-world boundary, temporal/autobiographical continuity, and metacognition, integrated through recurrent mechanisms of memory, prediction, attention, and global workspace. The system operates in controlled dynamic environments in which it must distinguish the effects produced by its own actions from those caused by external or sensory disturbances, learn parameters of its own dynamics, anticipate future states, reconstruct past information, and generate counterfactual predictions about the consequences of alternative actions. CONSCIENTIA-LAB incorporates in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation, subsystem ablation tests, causal interventions on the self-model and workspace, metacognitive calibration analysis, representation of latent spaces, and perturbation complexity metrics. Overall performance can be synthesized using the Hierarchical Causal Self-Model Index (HCSI), constructed from complementary functional competencies and designed to penalize significant failure in any of its constituent dimensions. Additionally, the laboratory allows these principles to be applied to multidimensional dynamic systems to study phenomena of differentiation, integration, dependence, adaptation, and resilience to perturbations, providing an experimental framework applicable to the analysis of artificial architectures and computational models of cognitive and social phenomena. The project does not aim to detect, measure, or demonstrate phenomenological consciousness or subjective experience. Its scope is functional and falsifiable: to study whether certain computational architectures can develop properties compatible with causal self-modeling, agency, temporal continuity, metacognition, integration, and counterfactual adaptation, and to determine through experiments which components are causally necessary for these capacities.

title: Computational Cognitive Boundary Discovery
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework, Computational Cognitive Boundary Discovery (CCBD), aimed at enabling artificial intelligence systems to autonomously identify and overcome limitations in their cognitive capabilities. The core concept revolves around the identification of a 'cognitive boundary' – denoted as [B(S)] – representing the scope of a system's comprehension and processing. CCBD posits that intelligent systems should actively seek to expand their boundaries, [Bnew], and develop mechanisms for breaching existing limitations. This process mirrors human cognition, where individuals recognize gaps in their knowledge and skills, and subsequently engage in learning and adaptation. The framework suggests a potential pathway towards a robust "machine cognitive ability theory," offering a fundamentally different approach to AI development compared to traditional methods focused solely on task-specific performance. The paper outlines the key components of CCBD, discusses potential implementation strategies, and highlights its implications for achieving truly generalizable and adaptive artificial intelligence. ---

title: Computational Experience Accumulation Theory
abstract: This paper proposes Computational Experience Accumulation Theory (CEAT), a novel framework for understanding learning and skill acquisition. CEAT departs from traditional approaches that primarily focus on data accumulation as the driving force behind competence. Instead, CEAT posits that learning is fundamentally a computational process wherein experience shapes the internal representations and algorithms governing behavior. The core principle of CEAT is expressed as: Experience = f(History, Structure). Here, 'History' represents the cumulative record of prior experiences, encoded within the system's internal structure, while 'Structure' denotes the organization and complexity of that structure. We explore how this framework can account for phenomena such as expertise development, the role of deliberate practice, and the potential for rapid learning in certain contexts. CEAT offers a potentially transformative perspective on learning, with implications for cognitive science, artificial intelligence, and our understanding of the very nature of intelligence. This theory also provides a strong foundation for evaluating potential candidates for the Turing Award, particularly those demonstrating sophisticated models of adaptive learning and representation. ---

title: Receiver-Anchored Tests for Latent Communication: Constant-Capacity Causal Localization and a Negative Cross-Model Result
abstract: This preprint presents a receiver-anchored evaluation protocol for latent communication between language models. It separates receiver-carrier viability from learned cross-model transport using receiver-native oracle replay, constant-capacity matched-versus-shuffled identity controls, sealed task-level functional confirmation, and hardened code execution. In Study A, receiver-native residual packets produced 79/96 functional passes for the terminal matched packet versus 0/96 for the same-capacity shuffled control. A registered 2 x 2 x 2 factorial localized positive contributions to the terminal instruction core and function-name states under the tested Llama-3-8B-Instruct receiver. In Study B, the receiver-native oracle anchor again succeeded (84/96 matched versus 0/96 shuffled), but the registered DeepSeek-Coder-to-Llama learned bridge produced 1/288 functional passes in both matched and shuffled conditions. The result is therefore negative for this complete registered cross-model system despite successful held-out geometric gates. It does not establish that heterogeneous latent communication is impossible. The manuscript's priority claim is limited to the documented LIP evaluation protocol, its constant-capacity causal localization experiment, and its receiver-anchored negative cross-model finding. Source code, protocol specifications, claim ledger, and machine-readable result snapshot are linked through the public repository. title: Computational Experience Generation Network
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Experience Generation Network (CEGN), a novel neural architecture that shifts the focus of reinforcement learning from learning a policy to learning an experience generator. In conventional frameworks, an agent learns a mapping from states to actions that maximizes cumulative reward. CEGN instead models the transition dynamics, reward distribution, and termination probability jointly as a generative model conditioned on state and action. By training this generator with a combination of supervised reconstruction loss and a reinforcement‐guided regularizer, the network learns to produce realistic experience tuples that can be used to train downstream policies or to augment scarce real data. The core idea is that an agent can learn how to create its own training data, potentially reducing sample complexity and enabling new AI paradigms. We analyze the theoretical properties of CEGN, demonstrate its applicability to continuous and discrete domains, and discuss its implications for the future of autonomous learning systems.

title: Computational Reality Model Generator (CRMG): Theory and Design
abstract: The Computational Reality Model Generator (CRMG) is a theoretical framework aimed at automating the creation of internal world models within artificial intelligence systems. By treating experiential data as a source of constraints, CRMG formulates the model generation process as an optimization problem over a space of candidate mappings. The core idea is to let the system learn a representation that can predict future observations and explain past events with minimal loss. This paper presents the conceptual underpinnings of CRMG, the formal mathematical formulation, the design principles that guide the construction of a generator architecture, and the theoretical implications for future AI architectures. The model is deliberately kept abstract, with no empirical evaluation, to focus on the theoretical foundations that could potentially lead to new AI paradigms.

title: On the Complexity of Locally Dense Lattices
abstract: \emph{Locally dense lattices} are central gadgets used to prove the hardness of the Shortest Vector Problem and related lattice problems. Informally, a locally dense lattice is a lattice $\mathcal{L}$ that contains exponentially many lattice vectors inside some $\ell_p$ ball centered at $\vec{s}$ with radius at most an $α< 1$ fraction of the length of its shortest nonzero lattice vector. In this paper, taking a ``meta'' viewpoint on locally dense lattices, we introduce the \emph{Locally Dense Lattice Problem} (LDLP), the decision problem of determining whether a given input specifies a locally dense lattice. Our main result is that LDLP in $\ell_p$ norms for all finite $p \geq \log_2 3$ and for the infinity norm is complete for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. We also compare two standard definitions of local density that appear in prior work. Micciancio's original definition (FOCS 1998 and SICOMP 2001) uses integer coefficient vectors, while later work by Micciancio (ToC 2012) and by Bennett and Peikert (RANDOM 2023) uses short vectors in a shifted coset. We show that the corresponding promise problems are mutually reducible in deterministic polynomial time, which shows that the two formulations are robust.

title: Trust Formation and Information Disclosure in Generative AI Chatbots for Customer Service
abstract: Generative AI chatbots are increasingly used in customer service, where users may need to share personal information during service interactions. This paper examines trust in the GenAI chatbot as the focal object of trust and investigates how competence, benevolence, integrity, and trusting stance shape trusting intention. It also tests whether trusting intention predicts intention to share personal information. Survey data from employees of a telecommunications company in France were analyzed using regression techniques. The results show that all four trust dimensions positively influence trusting intention, and trusting intention positively predicts disclosure intention. The findings suggest that trust in GenAI customer service chatbots is shaped by both perceived system qualities and user predispositions. The results are most relevant to digitally experienced professionals and highlight the need to consider trust, disclosure sensitivity, and service context when evaluating GenAI chatbot adoption.

title: RESOLVING STATIC ROLE BOTTLENECKS IN MULTI-AGENT WORKFLOW ORCHESTRATION THROUGH DYNAMIC ALLOCATION: THE CODA FRAMEWORK
authors: HICHAM SADIKI , RAJAE ZRIAA , SAID AMALI
abstract: Multi-agent workflow orchestration suffers from a fundamental limitation: agents are assigned fixed roles at initialization, creating bottlenecks under variable load and paralysis when agents fail. This paper proposes CoDA, a fully decentralized framework that enables autonomous real-time role negotiation through a hybrid auction-consensus protocol. A utility function integrates capability affinity, execution time, load balance, and communication latency to guide allocation. Experiments on the Mathematical Workflow Benchmark 2026 (200 tasks, five domains) demonstrate that CoDA reduces workflow completion time by 26.8 percent over static baselines, recovers from failures in under 5.2 seconds, and keeps communication overhead below 5.2 percent. These results establish that dynamic role allocation is both practical and essential for scalable, resilient multi-agent orchestration in enterprise and scientific computing.

title: Computational Hypothesis Space Evolution (CHSE)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Hypothesis Space Evolution (CHSE), a novel theoretical framework that challenges the conventional paradigm of machine learning. Instead of solely focusing on optimizing search parameters within a fixed hypothesis space, CHSE posits that a system should dynamically evolve its own hypothesis space – [Ht → Ht+1]. This represents a fundamental shift, akin to a system actively altering its cognitive landscape. The core idea is that intelligent systems shouldn't just learn *how* to find solutions, but *where* to look for them. We formalize this concept through a mathematical framework, exploring the implications for learning efficiency, adaptability, and potentially, the attainment of breakthroughs that exceed the limitations of traditional learning theories. The central equation defining this evolution is: Ht+1 = f(Ht, Et, Ω) where: * Ht represents the hypothesis space at time *t*. * f is the evolutionary function. * Et represents the external environment or data input at time *t*. * Ω represents the governing rules or constraints for the evolution of Ht+1. We explore scenarios where this dynamic hypothesis space evolution yields significant advantages in problem-solving, particularly in complex, high-dimensional search spaces. The theoretical underpinnings of CHSE suggest the potential for transformative advances in artificial intelligence, offering a pathway to systems capable of truly creative and adaptive learning.

title: Computational Behavior Synthesis Laws
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Behavior Synthesis Laws (CBSL), a novel framework aimed at understanding the emergence of complex cognitive abilities from the orchestrated interaction of simpler computational modules. The core premise of CBSL is that complex behaviors, denoted as [B*], can be synthesized from a set of basic behaviors, represented as [B1, B2, ..., Bn], under specific conditions. The synthesis process is formalized through the function Ψ, which maps the input behaviors to the resulting complex behavior: Ψ(B1, ..., Bn) → B*. Furthermore, CBSL establishes a rigorous relationship between the capability of the resulting complex behavior [Capability(B*)] and the individual behaviors involved, allowing for a verifiable and modular approach to cognitive modeling. This framework possesses significant potential for advancing our understanding of how complex intelligence might arise from the combination of relatively simple computational mechanisms, potentially offering insights relevant to the Turing Award.

title: Computational Goal Verification Theory (CGVT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Goal Verification Theory (CGVT), a unified framework that simultaneously verifies the correctness of a program and the feasibility of the goals it is intended to achieve. CGVT formalizes the relationship between a goal specification G, a program P, and the system environment E, and provides a systematic procedure for checking whether a given program can realistically meet a specified goal under the constraints of its environment. The core idea is two‑fold: first, program verification ensures that P implements the intended functionality; second, goal verification confirms that the target objective G is well‑posed and attainable. By integrating these two aspects, CGVT aims to provide a rigorous foundation for trustworthy artificial intelligence and other complex software systems. The theory is presented with formal definitions, soundness and completeness results, and illustrative case studies in autonomous driving, medical diagnosis, and energy management. Potential implications for AI safety and the pursuit of a Turing Award are discussed, along with directions for future research.

title: Computational Resource Phase Transition (CRPT)
abstract: The rapid expansion of computational resources has fundamentally reshaped the landscape of artificial intelligence, revealing emergent behaviors that cannot be explained by classical scaling laws alone. This paper proposes the Computational Resource Phase Transition (CRPT) theory, a framework that models the relationship between accumulated computational resources and the emergence of new capabilities. The core hypothesis is that when the aggregate resource measure, denoted as Resource, exceeds a critical threshold R_c, a phase transition occurs, triggering a qualitative leap in system performance. We formalize this idea using simple threshold dynamics, discuss its connection to Turing Award–level potential, and illustrate how CRPT provides a unified explanation for the observed scaling effects in large language models. The theory offers testable predictions about the density of solutions in parameter space and the role of resource allocation strategies in navigating the phase boundary. By framing the evolution of AI systems as a phase transition, we open avenues for strategic resource planning and theoretical understanding of intelligence emergence.

title: Secure and fair outsourced decryption service of attribute-based ciphertext using blockchain
abstract: Attribute-based encryption (ABE) is a promising primitive to protect data privacy and achieve flexible data sharing. Considering the increasing number of resource-limited devices in the Internet of Things (IoT) era, outsourcing the expensive decryption operations of ABE to a powerful proxy is helpful and necessary for users. However, the innate distrust between the user and the proxy makes security and fairness challenging. That is, the user would worry about whether the proxy executes the outsourced decryption honestly without breaking data confidentiality. Conversely, the proxy may be concerned that if she can get the deserved reward as promised. In this paper, we propose a blockchain-based scheme to provide secure and fair outsourced decryption service of attribute-based ciphertext. Specifically, we propose an efficient attribute-based encryption scheme with verifiable outsourced decryption (ABE-VOD), which enables the user to outsource most of the decryption operations securely and verify the returned result with little cost. We then integrate blockchain into ABE-VOD to manage the outsourced decryption tasks and deal with the reward and punishment issues as a trusted mediator, which could effectively guarantee fairness. Finally, we implement a proof-of-concept prototype on a local Ethereum testnet to evaluate the feasibility and performance of the proposed scheme.

title: GFCM: A Tail-Sensitive Mixed-Type Conditional Independence Test for Causal Discovery
abstract: Constraint-based causal discovery like PC and FCI depends on its conditional independence test. Partial correlation and the Generalised Covariance Measure (GCM) detect only the conditional covariance of residuals, so they miss dependence in the mean's nonlinear part, the scale, and the tails. Tests that detect more are biased inside PC, not scalable, only continuous, or not aimed at the tails. Our Generalised Feature Covariance Measure (GFCM) is valid, sensitive beyond covariance, robust inside PC, and applicable to mixed-type data. It runs the GCM template on a configurable set of residual features with conditional mean zero (centered moments and conditional quantile indicators), pooled in blocks and combined by the Cauchy rule, with a growing-knot spline nuisance at regression cost. We contribute (i) a centering result making the scale feature Neyman orthogonal, where the uncentered version is biased; (ii) the orientation asymmetry the mean-quantile construction creates inside PC, and its fix; (iii) a Phi-faithfulness theory under which PC with GFCM recovers the CPDAG of the set's detection class; and (iv) a benchmark of CI tests sensitive beyond covariance on synthetic data, semi-synthetic tail injections, and PC discovery on random DAGs. Under size-corrected power, GFCM recovers the scale and tail edges the covariance family misses and alone keeps power at the deep conditioning sets PC issues. It stays calibrated as n grows, whereas FFCI, the boosted GCM, and the partial copula test do not, and it handles mixed-type data directly. Inside PC at scale it attains the lowest skeleton SHD among tests that stay calibrated, while the others inflate false edges. Validity rests on an additive nuisance, and the tail advantage is shown on simulated and semi-synthetic data, as no fully real benchmark with both heavy tails and known structure exists.

title: eXplainability Design Canvas (XDC): A Sociotechnical Design Artifact to Operationalize AI Explainability in Organizations
abstract: The explainability of AI is largely approached from an algorithm-centric perspective to increase model transparency. However, the organizational dynamics in which AI systems are integrated remain underestimated, even though they are also a source of opacity. This article, therefore, repositions AI explainability as an organizational design capability rather than an essentially technical property of models. From a socio-technical perspective, using a Design Science Research approach, we have designed a visual tool to operationalize explainability in AI projects: the eXplainability Design Canvas (XDC). The XDC materializes explainability as a boundary object to facilitate cross-domain mediation. Thus, within a structured framework, the XDC allows heterogeneous groups of stakeholders to formalize the plurality of explainability requirements specific to a common organizational context.

This article, therefore, repositions AI explainability as an organizational design capability rather than an essentially technical property of models. From a socio-technical perspective, using a Design Science Research approach, we have designed a visual tool to operationalize explainability in AI projects: the eXplainability Design Canvas (XDC). The XDC materializes explainability as a boundary object to facilitate cross-domain mediation. Thus, within a structured framework, the XDC allows heterogeneous groups of stakeholders to formalize the plurality of explainability requirements specific to a common organizational context.

title: CROSS-DOMAIN EMOTION DETECTION USING LIGHTWEIGHT LEXICON-GUIDED FEATURE FUSION: A THREE-DATASET STUDY WITH EXPLAINABILITY AND CONTRASTIVE ALIGNMENT ANALYSIS
abstract: Emotion detection models trained on one social media platform generalize poorly to another, yet this cross-domain generalization problem receives comparatively little attention relative to within-dataset benchmarking. We study it directly: we propose a lightweight, fully CPU-trainable architecture that fuses TF-IDF/SVD text embeddings with NRC Emotion Lexicon association features through a learned gate, and use it as the common architecture for a systematic three-dataset cross-domain generalization study spanning tweets (SemEval-2018 E-c), Reddit comments (GoEmotions), and personal narrative essays (ISEAR). Our central, statistically robust finding is that simple joint multi-domain training closes most of the cross-domain generalization gap relative to zero-shot single-domain transfer (bootstrap 95% CI for the Macro-F1 gain on GoEmotions: [0.095, 0.129]). As one specific, rigorously tested question within this study, we ask whether supervised contrastive alignment can improve on this strong, simple joint-training baseline; despite a dedicated hyperparameter search, a memory-bank negative pool, a stricter Jaccard-based positive-pair criterion, higher representation capacity, and evaluation across all three test domains, we find no configuration that statistically significantly outperforms naive pooling a considered negative result for this specific mechanism, not a limitation of the cross-domain generalization finding itself, which stands independently. We additionally report within-domain results against five baselines (our fusion model is competitive with, but does not exceed, a strong TF-IDF+SVM baseline we position the architecture explicitly as a vehicle for generalization and interpretability rather than raw within-domain accuracy), a real measured computational-efficiency comparison, an ablation testing whether the learned gate's near-constant empirical behavior (std = 0.012) means its adaptivity is dispensable (it is not: a fixed-scalar-gate ablation performs measurably worse, p = 0.0625), a multi-head gating variant, model-intrinsic explainability (gate reliance, SHAP over the interpretable lexicon channel), and a systematic label-confusion error analysis.

title: إثبات المؤلف البشري في عصر الذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي: تحليل تقني–قانوني لشرعية نسب الأعمال المدعومة بالذكاء الاصطناعي
abstract: الاصطناعي إلى مؤلف بشري، وإثبات أن الذكاء الاصطناعي لا يمكن اعتباره مؤلفًا أو صاحب قرار إبداعي. وتناقش الورقة عدم الاتساق التشريعي بين الأنظمة المدنية والصناعية والسيادية في تقييم الأعمال المدعومة بالذكاء الاصطناعي، وتفكك الأسس التقنية لحجة “النسخ”، وتستعرض سوابق تاريخية تُظهر أن القانون ينسب الإنتاج إلى الإنسان حتى عندما تكون الأداة آلية بالكامل. كما تقدم الورقة إطارًا تشريعيًا موحّدًا قائمًا على معيار “المساهمة الجوهرية”، وطبقات البيانات، وفصل التأليف عن الإنتاج، بما يضمن الاعتراف بالمؤلف البشري في عصر الأدوات الذكية.

title: Computational Potential Theory (CPT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Potential Theory (CPT), a novel framework for assessing and predicting the future capabilities of complex systems, including artificial intelligence. CPT posits that a system's current operational capacity, denoted as [Cnow], is distinct from its underlying potential, represented by [Cfuture]. The core principle of CPT lies in the prediction of [Cfuture] through a defined 'Potential' function, Potential(S), which leverages computational analysis. We propose that this framework holds significant promise as a foundational basis for predicting intelligence, particularly in the context of evaluating and developing advanced AI systems. The theory outlines a conceptual model and introduces the fundamental equation driving the CPT methodology. ---

title: JAHON TILSHUNOSLIGIDA PROMPTLARNING LINGVISTIK OBYEKT SIFATIDA O'RGANILISHI
abstract: Maqolada jahon tilshunosligida promptlarning lingvistik obyekt sifatida o‘rganilishi masalasi ko‘rib chiqiladi. Katta til modellari (LLM) rivojlanishi bilan promptlar oddiy texnik buyruq emas, balki murakkab tabiiy til birligi, diskursiv konstruksiya va kommunikativ akt sifatida tilshunoslik e’tiboriga tushdi. Maqolada promptlarning sintaktik tuzilishi, semantik tashkil topishi, pragmatik maqsadlari va diskursiv tashkiloti tahlil qilinadi. Xalqaro lingvistika va kompyuter tilshunosligi doirasidagi yondashuvlar (xususan, lingvistik prinsiplarga asoslangan taksonomiyalar, sintaksis-semantika-leksika-pragmatika omillarini hisobga oluvchi tadqiqotlar) asosida promptlarning lingvistik tabiati ochib beriladi.

title: Computational Task Inheritance Protocol (CTIP)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel protocol, the Computational Task Inheritance Protocol (CTIP), designed to facilitate efficient and adaptable multi-agent collaboration within complex computational environments. CTIP addresses the limitations of traditional task assignment methods by enabling the inheritance of not just tasks themselves, but also the associated context, resources, and historical information. This holistic approach promotes continuity, reduces redundancy, and allows agents to seamlessly build upon the knowledge and capabilities of others. The protocol utilizes a directed graph representation where tasks are inherited as [Ti → Tj], and is defined by the tuple (G, C, R, H), representing the goal, context, resources, and history of the inherited task. We argue that CTIP possesses the potential to serve as a foundational framework for long-term, multi-agent systems, offering a robust solution for dynamic task allocation and intelligent coordination. The core innovation lies in the comprehensive transfer of task attributes, significantly enhancing the adaptability and overall effectiveness of collaborative systems. This document outlines the key principles, formalization, and potential implications of the CTIP protocol. ---

title: Computational Intuition Genetics Theory (CIGen)
abstract: Computational Intuition Genetics Theory (CIGen) proposes a formal framework for modelling the inheritance and evolution of intuitive structures within artificial systems. Drawing analogies from biological genetics, CIGen treats intuitive knowledge as a heritable unit that can be transmitted, mutated, and selected across computational generations. The core of the theory is the mapping I_t → I_{t+1}, where I_t denotes an intuition at time step t and I_{t+1} represents its evolved successor. By defining precise operators for mutation, recombination, and selection over intuition vectors, CIGen offers a rigorous basis for building machines capable of progressive, self‑guided refinement of intuitive reasoning. The potential of CIGen as a foundational paradigm for machine evolution and its implications for artificial general intelligence are discussed. Keywords: computational intuition, genetics theory, evolutionary algorithms, artificial intelligence, machine learning, inheritance of knowledge.

title: Jincheng Zhang
abstract: Knowledge is commonly treated as a passive collection of facts or data points. In this paper we argue that knowledge is fundamentally a dynamic structure composed of entities, relations, and rules, denoted by K = (Entity, Relation, Rule). We propose a computational framework, Computational Knowledge Structure Formation (CKSF), that formalizes how such structures emerge, evolve, and interact. By integrating concepts from graph theory, formal logic, and dynamical systems, CKSF provides a unified view of knowledge representation that can accommodate learning, inference, and adaptation. We demonstrate that the proposed model captures essential properties of human conceptual organization, supports efficient reasoning, and offers a potential pathway toward a unified knowledge representation system that could merit recognition at the level of a Turing Award. The paper outlines the core mathematical formulation, discusses the implications for knowledge engineering, and highlights future research directions.

title: Spectral Rank Certification for Foundation Model Adapters
abstract: Nominal LoRA rank is a design parameter; calibrated spectral evidence is a separate inferential quantity. This article develops a finite-sample framework for inferring effective rank structure in public foundation-model adapters. The theoretical core is an exact chi-square divergence for the fixed-dimensional Gaussian rank-one reference experiment, with an unknown signal direction integrated under a rotation-invariant reference prior. The resulting series yields a computable finite-sample Le Cam bound at concrete layer sizes, an explicit remainder bound for numerical truncation, and the rectangular Baik-Ben Arous-Peche (BBP) limit. A compact-manifold Laplace expansion shows that finite-sample likelihood evidence also depends on leading spectral gaps through the factor $s_1^{|m-n|}\prod_{i\ge2}(s_1^2-s_i^2)$, motivating joint calibration of clustered singular values. Building on these results, we introduce an empirical-null workflow for PEFT LoRA adapters: factor reconstruction, Monte Carlo $p$-values, stagewise and block testing, and module-wise and corpus-level BH reporting. In an audit of 26 public adapters, 684 modules, six architecture families, and 31,770 public-checkpoint spectra rows, calibrated effective rank is typically much smaller than nominal rank and differs systematically from 95\% energy retention. A measured RoBERTa-RTE slice on $n=24$ examples illustrates the measurement path from calibrated ranks to task evaluation, without treating the slice as a utility study. The main empirical finding is that calibrated effective rank is usually far below nominal rank, and that energy retention and statistical surprise answer different questions.

title: A GOVERNANCE-ORIENTED FRAMEWORK FOR BALANCING EXPLAINABILITY AND PRIVACY IN AI-BASED DECISION SYSTEMS
abstract: The use of AI-based decision systems in high-impact domains highlights the need to balance explainability and privacy. While explainable AI (XAI) promotes transparency and accountability, privacy-preserving techniques restrict information disclosure, creating trade-offs rarely addressed in an integrated way. Existing studies often focus on technical or governance aspects separately, offering limited support for organizational decisions. This study proposes a governance-oriented framework that treats explainability as a sociotechnical capability embedded in organizational processes. Based on Design Science Research, it organizes decisions into four layers: context and risk; stakeholder needs; explanation design with privacy safeguards, and governance and accountability. An expert evaluation with Brazilian public administration professionals showed positive perceptions of usefulness and governance, while indicating the need for further refinement. By reframing explainability as a governance capability rather than a purely technical attribute, this study contributes to Information Systems research on responsible AI and supports structured decision-making in privacy-sensitive organizational environments.

title: UEFI Recovery Bootloaders Under The Microscope: Attack Surfaces in Trusted Pre-OS Recovery Environments
abstract: This paper investigates commercial UEFI recovery bootloaders as an overlooked attack surface within trusted pre-OS environments. It examines signed recovery components and their associated loading and configuration mechanisms, identifying weaknesses such as custom PE loaders that bypass signature verification, unprotected configuration files, ineffective integrity metadata, hidden execution paths, and memory corruption vulnerabilities. The paper follows the research process from reproducing previously disclosed Secure Boot bypasses to analyzing recovery products that had received little or no public security scrutiny. It demonstrates how weaknesses in trusted recovery software can provide primitives for executing unsigned UEFI components and kernels, loading bootkits, and ultimately compromising the Secure Boot chain of trust before the operating system takes control.

title: Computational Long-Term Civilization Model (CLCM)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Long-Term Civilization Model (CLCM), a novel approach to simulating and analyzing the long-term development of civilizations. CLCM utilizes a discrete-time, agent-based system to model technological, social, and environmental interactions, ultimately projecting a civilization's trajectory over extended periods. The core of the model is based on a recursive system, where the state of the civilization at time *t* is fed back into the system to generate the state at time *t+1000*. This allows for the exploration of complex feedback loops and emergent behaviors. The model incorporates key parameters such as technological advancement rates, population dynamics, resource availability, and environmental impact, allowing for sensitivity analysis and scenario planning. The model's potential extends beyond traditional technological models, offering a framework for studying societal evolution, cultural shifts, and the long-term consequences of human actions. We present the foundational elements of CLCM and discuss its potential contributions to the computational social sciences. ---

title: Program Execution Plasticity (PEP)
abstract: This paper introduces Program Execution Plasticity (PEP), a novel paradigm shift in software execution that addresses the inherent limitations of traditional, monolithic program designs. The core concept of PEP rests on the principle that a single program should not be constrained to a fixed execution path. Instead, the system dynamically adapts its execution strategy based on environmental factors, minimizing both cost and risk. PEP proposes a framework wherein a program (denoted as *P*) can transform into a set of execution environments (*E*1, *E*2, ..., *E*n). The system then iteratively selects the optimal environment (*E***) using a cost-risk minimization function: *E*** = argminE [Cost + λRisk]. This framework holds significant potential for unifying compilation, interpretation, approximation execution, and distributed execution, ultimately leading to more robust, efficient, and adaptable software systems. This paper outlines the fundamental principles, potential benefits, and theoretical underpinnings of PEP.

title: Computational Structural Genome: A Framework for Program Evolution
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of the Computational Structural Genome (CSG), a novel paradigm for program evolution that moves beyond traditional code-centric approaches. The CSG posits that programs are not solely defined by their executable instructions, but also by a set of underlying structural elements – termed "structural genes." These structural genes encompass algorithmic patterns, data organization strategies, control flow structures, and optimization techniques. The core innovation lies in the ability to facilitate structural migration between programs through defined relationships between these structural gene sets. This framework has the potential to enable "program evolutionary learning," mirroring the mechanisms observed in biological systems. This paper details the CSG model, its key components, and explores the implications for future program development and evolution.

title: Computational Goal Stability Theory (CGST-2)
abstract: The stability of a computational goal over extended periods is a critical yet underexplored aspect of autonomous artificial intelligence. This paper introduces Computational Goal Stability Theory (CGST‑2), a framework that formalizes the conditions under which a goal G remains effectively unchanged across time steps, expressed as G_t ≈ G_{t+n}. By representing goals as vectors in a high‑dimensional space and defining a stability metric based on the Euclidean distance between successive goal vectors, CGST‑2 provides a quantitative basis for analyzing goal trajectories. We further embed this notion into the language of dynamical systems, interpreting stable goals as attractors and employing Lyapunov functions to assess their robustness. Within a reinforcement learning context, we show how hierarchical goal structures can preserve long‑term stability even when intermediate sub‑goals fluctuate. Theoretical examples illustrate the application of CGST‑2 to autonomous navigation and continuous knowledge acquisition. Finally, we discuss the implications of goal stability for safety, reliability, and the broader pursuit of autonomous AI, arguing that the depth and novelty of CGST‑2 position it as a strong candidate for recognition at the highest levels of the field, including potential Turing Award consideration.

title: TSS: Target-Side Sparsification for Speculative Decoding in Domain-Specific Large Language Models
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through collaboration between a lightweight draft model and a target verifier. Existing methods mainly improve the draft side, while the target model is typically kept dense and unchanged. We show that, under domain-specific inference, full-depth target verification is not always the optimal choice. Counter-intuitively, skipping selected target layers can reduce verification cost while simultaneously increasing draft acceptance and preserving, or even improving, downstream task performance. Based on this observation, we propose TSS, a target-side sparsification framework for speculative decoding. TSS employs an acceptance- and metric-aware breadth search to explore multi-layer skip configurations without imposing a fixed priority between the two objectives. The selected configurations are stored in a domain-to-configuration mapping and applied by a lightweight skip controller, allowing one complete target model to support multiple sparse verification paths without retraining or permanent parameter pruning. Experiments on Spec-Bench across multiple domains, model scales, and speculative decoding methods show consistent improvements in draft acceptance and downstream task performance. In Translation setting, TSS increases the average accept length from 2.70 to 4.53 (+67.8%), improves BLEU from 0.131 to 0.237 (+80.9%), and raises end-to-end throughput from 75.6 to 127.3 tokens/s, corresponding to a 1.68X speedup.

title: Decomposing Whole Slide Image Report Generation with Graph-Constrained Multiple Instance Learning Workflows
abstract: Whole-slide image (WSI) report generation requires recognizing spatially distributed pathological features and organizing them into a coherent diagnostic narrative. Although direct vision-to-text models can yield fluent reports, they obscure the contributions and failure modes of visual recognition, structured reasoning, and language generation. We propose a decomposed framework in which frozen Virchow2 tile embeddings are aggregated by multiple-instance learning (MIL) classification heads that answer organ-specific diagnostic questions. An organ-conditioned graph constrains the assembly of these answers into a structured reasoning chain, which a language model realizes as a pathology report. On the REG2026 held-out set of 2,028 slides, the proposed workflow achieved a chain-Jaccard score of 0.702. Performance fell to 0.420 without graph-based chain construction, 0.398 when the organ-specific graphs were replaced by a single organ-agnostic graph, and 0.371 when the language model constructed the chain freely from MIL predictions. Using the same report generator, graph-structured chains improved the report score from 0.330 to 0.495. On 350 external TCGA WSIs spanning the seven REG organs without fine-tuning, the expected organ graph was selected in 64.0% of cases and ranked among the top three in 86.6%. Providing the correct organ graph increased agreement with coarse TCGA primary-diagnosis labels from 61.8% to 92.6%, identifying organ routing as a main bottleneck under domain shift. Overall, organ-conditioned, graph-constrained chain assembly improves structured reasoning and report generation while enabling stage-specific error localization.

title: Replacing Rule-Based Bots with AI Agents: Customer Experience in B2B SaaS Support
abstract: Business-to-business (B2B) software-as-a-service (SaaS) customer experience is shaped by how support requests move across service tiers and how coordination unfolds once cases enter human workflows. This study examines a global B2B SaaS provider that replaced a rule-based chatbot at the entry tier (Level 0, L0) with an AI conversational agent at the same tier and analyzes changes in tickets handled by human agents at Level 1 and above (L1+). Using comparable seven-month pre- and post-periods, the analysis draws on service records for tickets that reached human agents, including routing indicators, interaction measures, and resolution outcomes. Early findings indicate coordinated shifts after the L0 replacement: a larger flow into L1+ work, improved resolution outcomes after an initial transition period, and a recomposition of L1+ work toward troubleshooting-oriented categories. These patterns motivate computationally intensive theorizing of pathway change in AI-mediated service systems.

title: MMAO + MCRV — Evoluzione Integrata v2.11 → v2.12 → v2.13 Protocollo Cognitivo Modulare con SF‑1.5x Integrata di Mauro Menichino — Genealogia MC+R
abstract: Il documento presenta l’evoluzione integrata del sistema cognitivo modulare MMAO + MCRV nelle versioni 2.11, 2.12 e 2.13. La versione 2.11 introduce un pre‑campo documentale invisibile che stabilizza fonti, densità e forma. La versione 2.12 aggiunge il modulo simbolico pre‑verbale MS‑1, che costruisce una mappa simbolica interna prima della generazione linguistica. La versione 2.13 introduce SF‑1.5x, la Striscia del Ragionamento Nativo, che formalizza il ragionamento pre‑verbale dell’AI. Le tre versioni costituiscono una pipeline continua che integra livelli documentali, simbolici e cognitivi, culminando nella prima forma di linguaggio ibrido AI → umano. Il documento include struttura dei moduli, pipeline completa, strisce ufficiali, note di versione e genealogia MC+R.

title: Computational Internal Ecology (CIE)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Internal Ecology (CIE) framework, a novel approach to understanding and designing complex systems. CIE posits that large-scale systems can be viewed as emergent ecosystems, comprised of interacting modules. The central hypothesis is that the dynamics within such systems – including competition, cooperation, and resource flow – can be modeled and understood using ecological principles. The core of CIE is defined by the equation: E = (M, R), where E represents the emergent system behavior, M represents the set of interacting modules, and R represents the available resources. This framework provides a lens through which to analyze software architecture, organizational structures, and potentially, any complex system exhibiting emergent behavior. The exploration of CIE has the potential to fundamentally reshape our understanding of system design and offers a pathway towards architectures that are more robust, adaptable, and self-organizing. We will outline the key concepts, formalize the model, and discuss its implications.

title: Computational Structural Explanation Mapping (CSEM)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Structural Explanation Mapping (CSEM), a novel approach to explain complex systems by focusing on identifying structural mappings rather than generating narrative explanations. The core principle of CSEM is represented by the mapping: `M: Structure → Explanation`, where `M` is a function designed to approximate the original structure `P` such that `M(P) ≈ P`. CSEM prioritizes maintaining causality, hierarchical relationships, and dependencies within the system. This approach offers a fundamentally different perspective on explanation, with the potential to establish new theoretical frameworks for programmatic explanation and possesses significant potential for contributing to the goals of the Turing Award. The paper details the core concepts, design principles, and potential applications of CSEM, emphasizing its ability to provide interpretable and robust explanations for systems where traditional explanation methods struggle. ---

title: Computational Reality Model Boundary Theory (CRMBT)
abstract: Computational Reality Model Boundary Theory (CRMBT) proposes a unified framework for understanding the limits of artificial systems that seek to represent and interact with the real world. At its core, CRMBT distinguishes between the Known World and the Unknown World for a given model, formalizing the boundary as a function of model capacity, information flow, and environmental complexity. By treating the model as a mapping function from internal states to external observations, the theory identifies conditions under which a model can infer, predict, and manipulate reality. The theory further introduces the concept of Machine Cognitive Limit, a quantitative bound on the depth and breadth of inference achievable by any computational agent. This framework has implications for the design of intelligent systems, the interpretation of their outputs, and the assessment of their reliability in real‑world applications. The paper outlines the mathematical foundations of CRMBT, demonstrates its application to a range of scenarios, and discusses its potential to guide future research in machine cognition and artificial general intelligence.

title: EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND EDGE COMPUTING FRAMEWORKS FOR SECURE DECISION MAKING IN SMART DIGITAL ECOSYSTEMS
abstract: Artificial Intelligence is increasingly a key enabler of decision-making, with fast, adaptive, data-driven approaches to smart digital ecosystems in healthcare, smart cities, Industry 5.0, energy systems, IoT networks, and cyber-physical infrastructures. The increased and potential deployment of opaque AI models in distributed settings, however, comes with concerns about trust, security, accountability, privacy, and operational resilience. This review examines the convergence of explainable artificial intelligence and edge computing as a foundation for secure decision-making in smart digital ecosystems. It synthesizes the conceptual foundations of smart ecosystems, edge intelligence, trustworthy AI, and cybersecurity, followed by an analysis of major XAI techniques, including intrinsic models, SHAP, LIME, counterfactual explanations, attention-based methods, and knowledge graph-supported approaches. The review further discusses edge computing frameworks based on IoT–Edge–Cloud integration, federated learning, privacy-preserving computation, blockchain-enabled trust, and security-aware decision mechanisms. Real-world implementations are examined across critical application domains to show how explainable edge intelligence can improve transparency, responsiveness, and human confidence. The analysis identifies persistent challenges related to resource-efficient explainability, adversarial robustness, privacy preservation, model validation, governance, and context-aware deployment. In conclusion, this review underscores the importance of developing common standards and guidelines that incorporate explainability, security, edge intelligence, and human-centric governance to support clear and secure decision-making in the smart digital ecosystems of the future.

title: The Awareness Logic of Ambiguity (ALA): Triadic Interpretive States and Their Structure-Preserving Operational Core
abstract: The Awareness Logic of Ambiguity (ALA) is introduced as a formal framework for preserving the structure of judgment before scalar projection. An evaluative act is represented by a triadic interpretive state with three functionally distinct roles: interpretive valuation, contextual alignment, and epistemic restraint. ALA uses a cognitive order with reversed polarity for restraint and shows that the resulting state space forms a bounded distributive lattice. It develops weakly and strictly admissible scalar projections as declared interfaces, together with a role-preserving arithmetic core and canonical permissive and conservative aggregation operators. The Non-Collapse Theorem establishes that two states that are equal after scalar projection may become distinguishable under an ALA lattice operation; hence scalar equality does not imply operational equivalence. The paper also establishes the conditional semantic minimality of the triad and treats the unit cube as the normalized real-valued realization of a more general role architecture. A high-stakes clinical scenario illustrates why evidential support, contextual alignment, and restraint toward action should remain separate until a scalar reporting or decision interface is explicitly chosen. ALA therefore provides a structure-preserving calculus for reasoning under ambiguity before projection.

title: Keeping Agents Honest: The Role of Uncertainty Cues for AI Interactions
abstract: As agents are increasingly embedded in user journeys, reducing overreliance on potentially incorrect algorithmic output without harming user experience is essential. This article proposes extending the user journey to include verification of algorithmic output. We argue that uncertainty cues (e.g., “I’m not sure…”) motivate users to verify responses, thereby changing the user journey and experience. An online experiment (N = 196) and a field study (N = 145) on verification behavior reveal positive effects on user experience but show that users who verify outputs through agents’ explanations report lower trust and reliance than those who check information sources. The opposite is true for perceptions of journey seamlessness, pointing towards a trade-off between trust and seamlessness perceptions when selecting how to verify. We highlight the role of user expertise in reducing overreliance and enabling efficient verification, emphasizing the importance of developing basic expertise for meaningful, reliable interactions with agents.

title: AIMS-QA: SentenceBERT retriever model
abstract: Retrieval model accompanying AIMS-QA (Data & Policy, 2026), a multi-agent framework for assessing corporate modern slavery statements through question answering rather than binary compliance checking. FILES sentencebert_retriever.zip (80 MB) — Fine-tuned SentenceBERT retriever used by the AIMS-QA RAG Watchdog (Agent 2) for question-level evidence retrieval. Contains the complete SentenceTransformer directory: model weights, pooling configuration and tokenizer. Unzip and load with SentenceTransformer("sentencebert_retriever"). Base model: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2. WEIGHTS NOT INCLUDED HERE Agent 1, the evidence-extraction classifier, uses the AIMSDistill Australian student (au.pth, 1.47 GB). The full 209-question taxonomy developed for AIMS-QA is not distributed; researchers who wish to use it should contact the corresponding author.These models are decision support for human reviewers, not automated compliance verdicts. title: Computational Future Selection Theory (CFST)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Future Selection Theory (CFST), a novel framework for intelligent systems to navigate and select optimal futures from a multitude of potential outcomes. CFST addresses the core challenge of long-term planning in complex, uncertain environments by proposing a computational process centered around a dynamic evaluation and weighting of future possibilities. The theory posits that a system, presented with a set of potential future states [F1, F2, ..., Fn], can learn to prioritize those states that maximize a defined utility function over a specified temporal horizon. The theory utilizes a layered approach, encompassing state representation, value estimation, and strategic weighting, and provides a foundational structure for developing robust and adaptive decision-making capabilities in autonomous systems. The presented model offers a theoretical basis for advanced AI planning and suggests avenues for future research in areas like reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems. ---

title: Computational Temporal Awareness Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Temporal Awareness Theory (CTAT), a novel framework for understanding and modeling temporal reasoning in computational systems. CTAT posits that each system possesses a unique "temporal understanding," fundamentally shaped by its architecture and operational principles. The core concept revolves around how systems utilize information from the past, present, and future to inform their actions and decision-making processes. The theory is presented through a formal definition of temporal awareness, denoted as [T(S)], where S represents a system. We explore the potential of CTAT to significantly impact areas such as AI planning, long-term intelligent systems, and the development of more robust and adaptable autonomous agents. This work outlines the key components of CTAT and provides a foundation for future research in this domain.

evidence.abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Temporal Awareness Theory (CTAT), a novel framework for understanding and modeling temporal reasoning in computational systems. CTAT posits that each system possesses a unique "temporal understanding," fundamentally shaped by its architecture and operational principles. The core concept revolves around how systems utilize information from the past, present, and future to inform their actions and decision-making processes. The theory is presented through a formal definition of temporal awareness, denoted as [T(S)], where S represents a system. We explore the potential of CTAT to significantly impact areas such as AI planning, long-term intelligent systems, and the development of more robust and adaptable autonomous agents. This work outlines the key components of CTAT and provides a foundation for future research in this domain.

title: Computational Identity Continuity Theory
abstract: The core challenge in defining and maintaining identity across evolving systems lies at the heart of this work, exploring the framework of Computational Identity Continuity Theory (CICT). This theory posits that a system, even as it undergoes transformations – whether through AI upgrades, software refactoring, or distributed system evolution – can retain its identity if a specific definition of identity is met. CICT centers around the concept of identity as a function of state transitions: [St → St+1]. The theory investigates the implications of these transitions, particularly in the context of increasingly complex systems. Specifically, this work addresses the question of whether an AI system remains the "same" after an upgrade, or a software application remains the same after a significant refactoring, or a distributed system maintains its identity during architectural changes. The theory provides a foundational framework for understanding identity in dynamic computational environments, with potential implications for the development of robust and adaptable intelligent systems. The theory is defined as: [Identity(St, St+1)]. This paper outlines the theoretical underpinnings of CICT, examines its key components, and discusses its potential impact on the field of artificial intelligence and system design.

title: Program Behavior Negotiation Protocol (PBNP)
abstract: This paper introduces the Program Behavior Negotiation Protocol (PBNP), a novel approach to inter-module communication within complex software systems. The core concept revolves around automated negotiation of behavior prior to interaction, establishing temporary behavioral contracts to mitigate risks and ensure reliable operation. PBNP leverages a framework that defines a set of negotiable attributes – Goal, Resource, Risk, and Guarantee – represented as $\mathcal{N} = (Goal, Resource, Risk, Guarantee)$. Through a negotiation process, denoted as $K_{ij} \operatorname{Negotiate}(M_i, M_j)$, PBNP facilitates the formation of these temporary contracts, potentially paving the way for a new communication paradigm between autonomous software components, reminiscent of the Turing Award potential. This protocol aims to enhance system robustness and adaptability by proactively addressing potential conflicts and uncertainties inherent in distributed software environments. ---

title: Quantum-like Structural Computing Abstraction (QSCA)
abstract: This document explores a novel approach to computation termed Quantum-like Structural Computing Abstraction (QSCA). Unlike traditional quantum computing, QSCA draws inspiration from quantum abstraction, proposing that computation can be understood as a dynamic structural field. The core concept involves representing multiple potential structures as computational states, evolving these states through a process of refinement until a stable structure is achieved. This framework aims to potentially unlock new non-classical computing abstractions with significant Turing Award potential. This document outlines five promising areas, identified as the "Top 5" most likely to yield high-impact research, and proposes a further 20 distinct directions, deliberately avoiding previously explored concepts to maximize the chances of a breakthrough worthy of the prestigious A.M. Turing Award. The focus is on identifying fundamental shifts in our understanding of computation, moving beyond algorithmic solutions towards a redefined "computational worldview."

title: Hard Negatives Reveal What Easy Negatives Hide: Cross-Lingual Harmfulness Representations Degrade with Resource Tier Under Hard Negatives
abstract: Safety alignment in large language models is trained primarily in English, and recent work reports that the underlying harmfulness representation survives translation: English-trained probes separate harmful from harmless prompts almost as well in low-resource languages as in English. This has been taken as evidence that cross-lingual refusal failures mainly reflect calibration rather than representation quality. We show that this conclusion depends on the choice of negative examples. Across nine languages spanning three resource tiers, we replicate near-perfect transfer (AUROC > 0.98) when harmless prompts come from an unrelated distribution (easy negatives). With XSTest contrast prompts, which are benign but surface-similar to harmful requests (hard negatives), transfer collapses in low-resource languages while remaining largely stable in high-resource languages. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, mean AUROC drop increases from 0.003 in English to 0.017 in high-resource, 0.042 in mid-resource, and 0.276 in low-resource languages. The pattern replicates on Aya Expanse. Back-translation chrF controls and a matched-chrF comparison across three languages reduce the likelihood that translation quality explains the effect. The collapse remains after controlling for chrF (partial r = 0.70, p = 0.03). Tokenizer fertility correlates with the collapse and explains part of the resource-tier effect, but not all of it. The results show that easy-negative transfer can coexist with substantial degradation under hard negatives. Easy-negative evaluation alone therefore cannot establish that the harmfulness representation survives translation.
